Moats in the AI Era

Strategy & Business — Competitive Strategy & Moats

A near-expert treatment of the question every board now asks: why a thin model wrapper has no moat, when "our data" is real, and how to convert an argument about adjectives into an argument about four measurable parameters.

1Two decisions, six weeks apart

On 4 September 2026, in a glass meeting room on the eleventh floor of an office tower in Lower Parel, Mumbai, Devika Raghunathan put a single slide on the screen and waited. She was Chief Product Officer of Yashvi Credit Systems, a four-and-a-half-year-old company that sold an AI underwriting co-pilot to non-banking financial companies and small finance banks. The slide showed two numbers: 62 lakh loan applications scored since launch, and 11.2 lakh of those applications for which Yashvi now knew, definitively, whether the borrower had gone ninety days past due. Across the table sat Farida Qureshi, a partner at a Mumbai growth fund that was three weeks into diligence on a ₹2,900 crore pre-money Series C. Qureshi's question was the one Raghunathan had been rehearsing answers to for a year. "A listed loan-origination-system vendor sits inside sixty lenders," Qureshi said. "It has more application flow than you do. It rents the same foundation models you rent. Tell me, with arithmetic, why it does not have your product by the end of next year."

Yashvi's numbers were good. Twenty-three lender customers, ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue growing at 71 percent, 68 percent gross margin after the cost of inference, bureau pulls and Account Aggregator fetches. The product read a borrower's bank statement flow through the RBI-regulated Account Aggregator rails, pulled GST returns where the applicant was a registered business, combined those with a bureau report, and returned two things: a risk score, and a structured memo explaining in plain language which four facts drove the score. Credit officers liked the memo more than the score. But Raghunathan knew that the memo — the part customers praised in reference calls — was the part a competent team could rebuild in a quarter with a good prompt and a schema. The score was different, and the difference was the whole argument she had to make.

Six weeks earlier and 1,400 kilometres north, Nandita Iyer had faced a decision that looked unrelated and was structurally the same. Iyer was Head of Product at Yuvraj Freight Exchange, a road-freight marketplace headquartered in Gurugram that matched 2,600 shipper accounts to 11,400 verified fleet operators averaging 4.2 trucks each. Yuvraj ran ₹3,180 crore of annualised gross merchandise value at a 7.4 percent take rate, 74,000 completed trips a month across roughly 1,900 active lane-pairs. Its AI layer did three things: it quoted a price for any lane within seconds, it predicted arrival time, and it ran an automated voice agent that made 96,000 check-calls a month to drivers in six languages at ₹4.30 a call against ₹31 for a human tele-caller.

On 24 July 2026 a global transport-management-system vendor had offered Yuvraj ₹46 crore over three years to license the lane-pricing model as an embedded API inside its Indian deployments — money equal to 19.6 percent of Yuvraj's net revenue, arriving at almost no marginal cost. The vendor's Indian installed base was about 400 shippers, perhaps 140 of whom Yuvraj's sales team had been chasing for two years. Iyer's founders wanted to take the cheque. Iyer's instinct said that selling the pricing model to the one party capable of assembling a rival exchange was selling the rope. Neither instinct was an argument. What follows is the analytical apparatus both executives needed, developed through their two situations, and it will return to their decisions at the end.

2The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree

A moat is a structural condition under which a competitor who can see exactly what you have built, wants to copy it, and has the resources to try, still cannot close the gap. Warren Buffett borrowed the word from castle architecture in his shareholder letters of the 1980s. Hamilton Helmer's 7 Powers (2016) gave it operating content by naming seven and only seven such conditions — scale economies, network economies, counter-positioning, switching costs, branding, cornered resource and process power — and insisting that each must simultaneously confer a benefit to you and impose a barrier on the copier. Helmer's discipline matters here: "we have proprietary data" is not a power, because it names an asset rather than a barrier. It becomes a power only when you can say which of the seven it instantiates and what specifically the copier cannot do.

The deeper root, and the one that explains the AI era better than Helmer does, is David Teece's 1986 paper Profiting from Technological Innovation. Teece's question was why innovators so often fail to capture the value of their own inventions, and his answer was that when an innovation is easily imitated and no intellectual-property regime protects it, the returns flow not to the inventor but to whoever owns the specialised complementary assets the innovation needs to reach a customer. Teece wrote about manufacturing capacity and distribution channels. Substitute "a rentable frontier model" for the innovation and the framework reads as if it were written for 2026: the capability is universally available, therefore the surplus accrues to whoever holds the scarce complement. The strategic question is not what your model can do. It is what your model needs that other people cannot get.

Four schools now argue about what those scarce complements are, and it is worth stating what each would and would not sign, because a general manager refereeing a disagreement between two competent practitioners is usually refereeing a collision between two of these.

The powers-are-invariant school holds that artificial intelligence changes the identity of who holds which power but changes nothing about the list. It would sign: "no advantage is durable unless it instantiates one of the seven powers, and data is a route to a power, never a power itself." It would not sign: "data network effects constitute an eighth power." Its evidentiary base is the recurrence of the same seven mechanisms across steam, electricity, packaged software and cloud.

The conditional-data school, whose canonical statement is Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright's 2020 Harvard Business Review article "When Data Creates Competitive Advantage," argues that usage data produces advantage only under a conjunction of conditions: the data must be proprietary, its marginal value must not saturate quickly, it must decay slowly enough to be worth accumulating, and the improvement it buys must be something customers notice. It would sign: "a data advantage is real but conditional and usually narrower than claimed." It would not sign: "more data is monotonically better," which is the proposition most pitch decks quietly assume.

The distribution school descends from Ben Thompson's Aggregation Theory (2015) and from Clayton Christensen's law of conservation of attractive profits: when one layer of a stack commoditises, profits migrate to the adjacent layer that is now scarce. It would sign: "when supply is commoditised, the firm owning the demand relationship captures the surplus, and AI has commoditised a great deal of supply." It would not sign: "a specialist with a materially better model can take a category from an incumbent aggregator on quality alone." This school reads Yuvraj's licensing offer as free money and reads Yashvi's memo quality as irrelevant.

The capability-scaling school takes its text from Richard Sutton's 2019 essay The Bitter Lesson and from the scaling-law literature beginning with Kaplan and colleagues in 2020 and refined by the Chinchilla results in 2022. Its claim is that hand-built structure, domain heuristics and narrow fine-tuning are repeatedly eaten by the next general model trained with more compute on more data. It would sign: "most vertical fine-tuning advantages have a half-life of two to four model generations." It would not sign — and this exception is the hinge of the entire page — "outcome data that exists nowhere in any pretraining corpus will also be eaten," because no amount of general-purpose compute can tell you which of Yashvi's borrowers actually defaulted.

The disagreement is not about whether data can be a moat. It is about which kinds of data sit outside the reach of the next model, and how narrow that set really is.

3Mechanics in depth: four parameters, worked through

Expert practitioners do not argue about whether "our data" is a moat. They decompose the claim into four parameters, each of which can be estimated from data a company already has, and then they compute a time-to-parity. The four are flow ratio, label latency, density threshold, and acquisition rights. Everything else in the debate is commentary on these.

Parameter one: flow ratio, and the parity formula

Let your accumulated stock of useful training signal be S, and let your current monthly inflow be f. Define T = S / f, the number of months of accrual at today's rate that your stock represents — Yashvi's T is 26, Yuvraj's is 31. Let r be the rival's monthly inflow as a multiple of yours. If the rival starts from zero and both of you keep accruing, the rival reaches a fraction φ of your stock at time t, where r·f·t = φ·f·(T + t), which rearranges to t = φT / (r − φ). At full parity, φ = 1 and the formula collapses to the more famous t = T/(r−1): if the rival's inflow exceeds yours, your lead has a finite, computable expiry; if it does not, you are never caught. The naive version of "we have twenty-six months of data" assumes the rival must also take twenty-six months. The formula says otherwise. The listed origination vendor inside sixty lenders carries roughly 3.2 times Yashvi's application flow. At φ = 1 it reaches parity in 26/2.2 = 11.8 months.

Parameter two: label latency, the only variable capital cannot buy

Here the two protagonists diverge, and the divergence is the most useful thing on this page. Yuvraj learns whether its price quote was right within about four days: the trip completes, the invoice settles, the realised rate is known. Yashvi learns whether its risk score was right after eleven months on average, because a loan must season before ninety-days-past-due is meaningful. Applications are not labels. A rival can buy application volume with distribution; it cannot buy the passage of time. Label latency L therefore adds to the parity clock rather than dividing into it: effective time-to-parity is φT/(r−φ) + L.

Run it for Yashvi at φ = 0.35, which is the level at which, as parameter three shows, the rival becomes commercially adequate rather than equal. The formula gives 0.35 × 26 / (3.2 − 0.35) = 9.1/2.85 = 3.2 months of application accrual, plus 11 months of seasoning, for 14.2 months. That is uncomfortably short, and it was the honest first answer Devika Raghunathan's team computed in June 2026. The number only improved when they modelled parameter four.

Parameter three: density threshold, or why advantage is decision-shaped, not company-shaped

Learning curves in most applied settings are power laws: error falls roughly as error ≈ a · N−b, with b commonly between 0.2 and 0.35 for tabular prediction and for the kind of demand forecasting Yuvraj does. Take b = 0.3. Halving your error requires 21/0.3 ≈ 10.1 times the data. Read the same equation from the rival's side and it says something that should unsettle anyone who has ever put "10x more data than competitors" on a slide: a rival with one-eighth your data has error only 80.3 ≈ 1.87 times yours, not eight times. With one-tenth your data it is within a factor of two. Data advantages do not scale linearly; they compress logarithmically. Whether that compressed advantage is worth anything depends entirely on where the customer's tolerance threshold sits relative to both of you.

And the unit that matters is not the company. It is the smallest unit over which the model must generalise — a lane, a borrower segment, a SKU, a disease code. Yuvraj's aggregate data looks formidable and its lane-level data does not. Its top 40 lanes carry 48 percent of trips and its top 120 carry 71 percent; the remaining 1,780 lanes split the rest. Mean absolute percentage error on quotes is 5.2 percent on the top 40, 6.1 percent on the top 120, and 19.4 percent across the tail. Yuvraj's own commercial research puts the shipper tolerance threshold at about 9 percent, the point at which calling two brokers beats accepting the exchange's quote in expectation.

Yuvraj's quote-accuracy advantage is commercially meaningful only in the band where it clears the 9 percent shipper-tolerance line and a plausible rival does not — roughly lanes 40 to 300, about 23 percent of trips. Above that band both parties are good enough and accuracy stops being a reason to choose; below it neither party is good enough and shippers negotiate by phone regardless. Reading the company average of 8.9 percent would have told Iyer nothing about any of this.

The rival curve in Figure 1 is not a guess. A new entrant concentrating on head lanes routes about 55 percent of its volume onto the top 40 against Yuvraj's 38 percent, so at 12 percent of Yuvraj's aggregate volume its effective per-lane density on those lanes is 0.12 × (0.55/0.38) ≈ 0.17 of Yuvraj's. Applying the power law, its error there is 0.17−0.3 ≈ 1.69 times Yuvraj's 5.2 percent, or 8.8 percent — just inside the tolerance threshold. In the lanes that carry nearly half of all Indian long-haul freight on this exchange, a rival with one-eighth the data is already good enough. That single calculation reframes the licensing decision Iyer faced more sharply than any qualitative debate about strategy could.

Parameter four: acquisition rights, the part that is actually cornered

The fourth parameter is legal and contractual, and it is where Yashvi's answer to Farida Qureshi eventually came from. Under the RBI's digital lending guidelines and the consent architecture of the Account Aggregator framework, and now under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, borrower data obtained for underwriting one lender's loan cannot be freely pooled to train a model that serves a different lender unless the contract and consent artefact permit exactly that. Yashvi's founders, negotiating in 2022 and 2023 from a position of no leverage whatsoever, had asked for a narrow "model improvement" clause permitting aggregated, de-identified outcome labels to inform a shared risk model. Nineteen of twenty-three lenders signed it, largely because in 2022 nobody thought it was worth fighting over. Yashvi's data-science lead in Bengaluru, Aparna Sen, estimated that a rival attempting the same clause in 2026 — after every lender's legal team had read three years of commentary on data as a strategic asset — would win it from perhaps 55 percent of accounts and would spend nine months of contracting to do it.

Feed that back into the parity arithmetic. Consent-constrained flow drops the rival's effective r from 3.2 to roughly 1.9, so t = 0.35 × 26 / (1.9 − 0.35) = 5.9 months; add eleven months of label seasoning and nine months of renegotiation that must largely precede collection, and the practical answer stretches from 14 months to about 26. Twenty-six months is not forever. It is, however, long enough to convert into something more durable, which is precisely what a moat is for.

4When the framework applies, and when it actively misleads

The four parameters can be stated as testable claims, and the discipline of applying each to both protagonists is what turns a framework into a decision. Claim one: the advantage is real only if the rival's inflow ratio r is below the level at which parity arrives inside your planning horizon. For Yashvi, r is high and the claim fails on flow alone; the company is rescued by latency and rights, not by volume. For Yuvraj, r against a serious TMS-backed entrant is low today but would rise sharply the moment Yuvraj licensed its pricing model and handed that entrant a cold-start solution. Claim two: label latency protects only where the label is genuinely delayed and genuinely unavailable elsewhere. Yashvi passes; Yuvraj fails, because realised freight rates leak into the market within days through brokers and through e-way-bill-derived movement data. Claim three: the advantage must survive at the decision-unit level, not the company level. Yuvraj passes only on a band of roughly 260 lanes; Yashvi passes on its two largest borrower segments and fails on new-to-credit applicants, where it has 41,000 matured labels against the 300,000 its own team considers the minimum for stability. Claim four: the acquisition right must be exclusive in practice. Yashvi passes through its 2022-vintage contract clauses; Yuvraj fails, because any fleet operator may list on three exchanges simultaneously and frequently does.

The framework misleads in three identifiable situations. The first is when the customer's problem is not accuracy at all. Roughly a third of Yashvi's renewal value, by its own win-loss analysis, comes from audit trail: the structured memo satisfies an internal credit-committee documentation requirement, and a lender that has passed an RBI inspection with Yashvi's memos in the file has a reason to stay that has nothing to do with model quality. Analysing that advantage as a data moat gets the answer wrong twice — it understates durability and misdirects the investment.

The second is when the market is growing faster than anyone's loop. In a category expanding at 60 percent a year, a rival can build a large business entirely out of customers you have not reached, and your beautifully defended position protects a shrinking share of the prize. The third is when the advantage is real, defensible and small. Yuvraj's live band covers 23 percent of trips; if the founders reorganised the company around defending it, they would be optimising a moat around a pond.

5Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

The clean two-party story breaks in five recognisable situations, and mature companies handle them differently from how they describe handling them.

Multi-product. Yashvi's obvious second product is a collections prioritiser: which delinquent accounts to call first. Executives assume the underwriting label stock transfers. It transfers badly. An underwriting label answers "would this applicant have defaulted"; a collections label answers "did this intervention change the outcome", which is a causal question requiring randomised holdouts Yashvi never ran. The company's 11.2 lakh labels reduce to roughly 60,000 usable observations for the new decision. The tell that an organisation has not noticed this is a product roadmap that lists adjacent products in the order of market size rather than in the order of label transferability.

Two-sided. In a marketplace the AI layer almost never creates the moat; it amplifies or leaks the one liquidity already provides. Yuvraj's pricing model exists because its trips exist. Licensing it is therefore not a product decision but a decision to convert a stock of liquidity-derived advantage into a flow of cash while simultaneously lowering the cold-start cost for the buyer. Both effects are real; the honest question is the exchange rate between them.

Regulated. Regulation is a two-sided moat, and practitioners consistently model only one side. The purpose-limitation regime that makes it hard for Yashvi's rival to pool lender data also caps Yashvi's own loop: four of its twenty-three customers refused the model-improvement clause, and those four represent 21 percent of its application volume and, awkwardly, the highest-quality data in the portfolio. A company that celebrates regulation as a barrier without measuring the tax it pays on its own flywheel has done half the analysis.

Hardware plus software. Yuvraj considered subsidising GPS units into fleet operators' cabs to secure exclusive telematics. The arithmetic is seductive and usually wrong in India, because the National Highways Authority's FASTag toll reads and the GST e-way-bill system already publish a coarse movement signal to every participant. Paying ₹2,900 a unit across 11,400 operators to buy a finer version of a signal that is becoming a commons is how companies convert capital into a depreciating advantage. Hardware creates a moat when it produces a signal that has no public substitute and when the installed base itself imposes switching costs; a GPS puck satisfies neither condition well.

AI-native. The hardest case is a company whose entire product is the model, with no workflow, no system of record and no contractual rights to fall back on. Such a company's moat parameters are all set by other people: its flow ratio depends on whoever distributes it, its latency is zero, its density threshold is defined by a general model that improves monthly. This is the structural reason the thin-wrapper critique bites. The critique is not that wrappers are lazy — many are excellent, and shipping one first is a perfectly sound opening move. It is that a wrapper's four parameters are all exogenous, so it has no schedule of its own.

At the organisational seams, three failures recur. Label quality degrades where the data-platform team owns the pipeline and the product team owns the roadmap, because nobody's objective function includes the freshness of the outcome join. Legal owns the consent language that determines whether the moat is usable at all, and is usually briefed to minimise risk rather than to maximise rights. And sales, compensated on bookings, will trade away data rights for a discount without anyone pricing what was traded. Mature companies do not solve this by exhortation; the ones that handle it well give a single named executive a standing agenda item on data rights, put a clause-level checklist into the contract template, and review quarterly which accounts have degraded rights. Publicly they say they have a data moat. Internally, what they actually defend is contract duration, integration depth, procurement inertia and the audit trail — and they treat model quality as table stakes they must not lose rather than as the advantage they will win on.

6Ten nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: "proprietary" is a property of the rights, not of the bytes. Competent practitioners audit what data they hold; experts audit what they are permitted to use, for what purpose, for how long, and whether that permission survives a change of control or a customer's exit. The tell in the wild is a company that can produce a data-volume dashboard in thirty seconds and cannot say, without asking legal, which contracts allow cross-customer model training. The obvious reading — that holding the data is the hard part — is backwards; obtaining the right to use it is the part that took Yashvi three years and cannot be repeated on the same terms.

Two: the advantage is decision-unit shaped. Aggregate data volume is almost always a misleading statistic because models generalise over units, not over companies. The tell is a board deck reporting total records with no distribution by segment. Figure 1 is the general case: advantage concentrates in a band and vanishes above and below it. The obvious reading — more total data means more advantage everywhere — ignores that the head is where everyone is already good enough and the tail is where nobody is.

Three: power-law scaling means advantages compress, and the customer's threshold decides whether the residue is worth anything. One-eighth the data buys 87 percent more error, not 700 percent. The tell is a team that reports its own accuracy curve and has never estimated the rival's. The obvious reading — that a 10x data lead is a 10x quality lead — is arithmetically false under every scaling exponent ever measured.

Four: label latency is the only parameter money cannot compress. Capital buys distribution, engineers, GPUs and data-licensing deals. It cannot buy the eleven months a loan needs to season, the two years a cancer-screening cohort needs to mature, or the eighteen months an enterprise churn signal needs to resolve. The tell is a competitor announcement that a team reads as catastrophic and an expert reads as an eleven-month delay. The obvious reading — that a well-funded entrant closes any gap — mistakes money for time.

Five: a moat that depends on the base model staying weak is a short position on the frontier labs. Yashvi tracks two deltas separately: the gap between a vanilla model and its tuned system on memo quality, a capability delta; and the gap on default prediction, an outcome delta. Across three base-model generations the capability delta fell from an index of 100 to 29 while the outcome delta stayed flat. The tell is an engineering roadmap dominated by prompt and scaffold work. The obvious reading — that model progress helps you because your product improves — forgets that it helps every rival by exactly the same amount, and helps them more if their deficit was structural rather than informational.

Memo quality was a capability the base model could learn from the public corpus; ninety-day delinquency on Yashvi's specific borrowers exists in no corpus at all. An expert looks at this chart and stops funding the red line.

Six: switching costs made of consequence outlast switching costs made of friction. Friction-based lock-in — data trapped in a proprietary export format, a painful migration — is fragile, resented and increasingly illegal as data-portability provisions of the DPDP Act take effect. Consequence-based lock-in arises when leaving means accepting a worse outcome the customer must then explain: a credit committee that must justify to an inspector why it changed a working underwriting process. The tell is how renewal conversations are won: by the account manager, or by the risk head. The obvious reading — that lock-in is lock-in — misses that one kind compounds with trust and the other corrodes it.

Seven: counter-positioning is the most under-used power in the AI era. When an incumbent's revenue comes from per-seat licences or from billable human hours, it cannot match an outcome-priced AI product without cannibalising itself, and its inability is structural rather than a failure of nerve. Yashvi's origination rival charges per seat; pricing underwriting per correct decision would collapse its own comparables. The tell is an incumbent that ships the feature quickly and then prices it in a way that protects the old line. The obvious reading — that a larger competitor with the same technology must win — ignores that its business model is a constraint it cannot relax quickly.

Eight: a flywheel must be cost-negative, not merely accuracy-positive. Every additional record has a storage, labelling, monitoring and retraining cost, and in regulated domains a compliance cost. Yashvi spends roughly ₹2.30 per scored application on data operations against ₹34 of price. If accuracy improvements slow along the power law while operating costs rise linearly with volume, the flywheel silently becomes a cost centre that the company continues to describe as a moat. The tell is a cost-per-record line that nobody in product can quote.

Nine: distribution and data are substitutes over a decade and complements over a quarter. The distribution school and the data school talk past each other because they use different horizons. Within a quarter, distribution decides who gets the customer and data decides who keeps them. Over five years, a distribution advantage that never converts into a data or switching-cost advantage decays as channels fragment, and a data advantage that never buys distribution starves. The tell is a strategy document that names only one of the two.

Ten: the moat question is frequently a valuation question wearing a disguise. When Farida Qureshi asked what stops the origination vendor, she was not asking for a technical answer; she was asking what gross margin and net revenue retention would look like in year seven, because those are what a 30x multiple is a claim about. Experts answer the question that was asked, in the units of the questioner: a moat argument that does not end in a margin or a retention number has not landed. The tell is a defensibility slide with no number on it.

7How this differs across product types and company stages

Across product types, the four parameters do not change; which one binds changes. In consumer products, switching costs are near zero and label latency is near zero, so parameter three usually binds: the question is whether per-user personalisation density ever crosses a threshold the user can feel. Most consumer AI features never do, which is why the category is won on distribution and brand. In B2B and enterprise, parameter four binds most often: the constraint is not whether you can build the model but whether your contracts let you learn from what the model saw. In platforms and marketplaces, parameter one binds through liquidity, and the AI layer is a multiplier on an advantage created elsewhere; a marketplace with no liquidity and a brilliant matching model has nothing to multiply. In hardware and physical goods, latency is long and label acquisition is expensive, which makes parameter two unusually protective — but only where no public commons is converging on the same signal. In AI-native products all four parameters are exogenous, which is the precise sense in which a thin wrapper has no moat.

It is worth saying plainly where the differences are not real. The claim that "enterprise AI is defensible and consumer AI is not" is folklore: an enterprise company with weak data rights and fast labels is exactly as exposed as a consumer app, and Yashvi's own new-to-credit segment is undefended despite being enterprise-sold. The claim that regulated industries are automatically safer is likewise half-true and dangerous, because regulation taxes your loop as surely as it taxes the entrant's.

By stage, the pattern is more consistent. A seed-stage company should not attempt to have a moat; it should attempt to have a customer, while taking one cheap, irreversible action — asking for the data-rights clause when nobody is fighting for it, which is free at seed and costs nine months at Series C. At Series A and B, the task is to compute the parity schedule honestly and to spend the remaining months converting a head start into a power; a company that still answers the defensibility question with a time-to-market story at Series B has spent the runway. At Series C and beyond, the moat is expected to show up in the numbers, as net revenue retention, gross margin and win rate against the named incumbent, and an architecture argument no longer substitutes. For incumbents, the characteristic error is the opposite: assuming that an existing bundle-level moat automatically extends to a bolted-on AI feature, when a specialist can lose the bundle war and still win every feature-level evaluation for three years.

8Three worked examples, including one that failed

Example one: Yashvi's economics, and what the moat is actually worth. Consider a representative customer, a mid-sized NBFC disbursing ₹100 crore a month at an average ticket of ₹1.2 lakh. Its incumbent stack — bureau score plus policy rules plus a general model reading bank statements — approves 31.0 percent of applicants while holding twelve-month credit losses at 4.0 percent. Yashvi's model, at the same 4.0 percent loss ceiling, approves 38.5 percent. That is ₹24.2 crore of additional monthly disbursal at unchanged risk. At a 4.2 percent contribution margin over the roughly fourteen-month average loan life, each monthly cohort is worth about ₹1.02 crore, or ₹12.2 crore annualised. Yashvi prices at ₹34 per scored application plus 0.18 percent of disbursal, which for this lender is about ₹31.5 lakh a month, or ₹3.78 crore a year. Value created to price captured is 3.2 to 1 — wide enough that the customer does not shop, narrow enough that Yashvi is visibly leaving money on the table, which is the shape a defensible position tends to have while it is still being built.

Example two: Yuvraj's licensing arithmetic. The TMS vendor's ₹46 crore over three years is worth about ₹38 crore on a present-value basis at Yuvraj's cost of capital, and it drops almost entirely to contribution. Against that, Iyer's team modelled the liquidity effect. The vendor's 400 Indian shippers ship roughly ₹9,600 crore a year in aggregate. Historical conversion suggested Yuvraj would win 6 to 8 percent of that volume onto its exchange over three years through its own sales motion — call it ₹690 crore of GMV, ₹51 crore of net revenue at a 7.4 percent take rate. If embedding Yuvraj's pricing inside the vendor's product removed the primary reason those shippers would migrate, the licence would cost more than it paid, and it would do so by funding a competitor's cold start: the vendor's own realised-rate data, once its customers transacted on its quotes, would raise its effective r from 0.12 towards 0.6, collapsing the five-month parity estimate in Figure 2 to something closer to eighteen months of total exposure rather than a permanent gap. Iyer's counter-proposal was the expert move: license the ETA model, not the pricing model. The ETA advantage rests on telematics and e-way-bill signals that FASTag and GSTN feeds are steadily commoditising anyway — an asset with a visible decay curve — while lane pricing rests on realised-rate data that only Yuvraj's own liquidity produces. Monetise the decaying asset; keep the compounding one.

Example three: Yamini Studio, and what recovery actually looked like. Yamini Studio was founded in Pune in early 2024 around a genuinely clever consumer product: a vernacular short-video captioning and dubbing app that let a creator record in Marathi and publish in six languages. It raised ₹31 crore, reached 8.4 lakh monthly active users by November 2024 on the strength of onboarding design and a much-shared launch, and monetised at about ₹14 per user per month on a 4 percent paid conversion. It was, by its founder Karthik Menon's own later account to his investors, a thin wrapper: a speech model, a translation model, a voice model, and 4,000 lines of orchestration. In February 2025 a large consumer platform shipped the same capability inside a surface hundreds of millions of Indians already had open. Yamini's monthly actives fell from 8.4 lakh to 1.6 lakh over five months. Every one of its four parameters was catastrophic, as Table 2 records: a rival flow ratio above 180, zero label latency, no meaningful decision unit over which its data could specialise, and no exclusive right to anything.

The recovery is instructive precisely because it was modest. Menon stopped defending the model and started building an asset nobody else held: for regional FMCG distributors running district-level advertising, Yamini assembled a brand-asset library — approved logos, mandated legal disclaimers, distributor-specific pricing overlays, and a two-stage human approval workflow that produced a compliance record. The generation quality was frankly no better than the free alternative. What the customer could not get elsewhere was the library, the approval trail and the integration into their existing creative sign-off. By June 2026 Yamini had 340 paying business accounts at an average ₹11,000 a month, about ₹4.5 crore of ARR, with churn under 2 percent monthly. The company recapitalised at ₹48 crore post-money against a peak paper value of ₹190 crore. The moat is real and small; the founders describe the outcome as a business rather than a vindication. The lesson worth taking is not "pivot to B2B." It is that the asset Yamini eventually defended — a customer-specific library plus an approval workflow that creates consequence-based switching cost — was buildable in month three and was not built, because in month three the team believed the model was the product.

9Failure modes, their early warnings, and the cost of late diagnosis

Six failure modes recur often enough to be worth naming with their diagnostics. Proxy-label drift occurs when the label you train on stops tracking the outcome you sell; its early warning is offline accuracy improving while the commercial metric — approvals at constant risk, quote acceptance — does not move for two consecutive quarters. The diagnostic question is simply: when did we last confirm that the label and the customer's outcome are the same thing? Caught early it costs a re-labelling sprint; caught after a pricing change built on it, it costs a customer's credit policy.

Selection-biased feedback is the most dangerous mode in lending and the least visible. Yashvi only observes outcomes for loans that were approved, so its model becomes progressively better at scoring the population it already likes and progressively blind at the approval boundary. The early warning is a rising error rate specifically in the newly-approved band; the diagnostic is whether any randomised holdout exists at all. Yashvi funds a deliberate 0.4 percent random-approval sleeve — roughly 640 loans a month and about ₹1.9 crore of expected annual loss — as the price of an unbiased signal. Competent teams regard that as waste; experts regard it as the cost of keeping the flywheel honest, and the cost of discovering its absence late is a model that fails precisely when the lender expands its credit box.

Company-level moat accounting shows up as aggregate record counts in board material with no distribution by decision unit, and it is caught by asking for the segment-level version of Figure 1. Inertia mistaken for switching cost announces itself when renewals are increasingly won by relationship and discount rather than by risk-owner preference; the diagnostic is to ask what the customer would have to explain to whom if they left. Worthless exclusivity is the mode where a company pays for a dataset the base model already contains, and its early warning is that no one ran the obvious experiment — measure vanilla model performance on the task before signing the data deal. Unmonitored capability-delta decay, finally, is caught by running the vanilla baseline as a standing item in every release evaluation, which costs a day per model generation and, if skipped, produces the specific experience of discovering in a competitive bake-off that the feature you invested two years in is now free.

10Where thoughtful people still disagree

Four disagreements in this field are genuine, and a product leader should be able to argue both sides of each.

Is data a power or merely a route to one? The Helmer-orthodox position is that data is an asset and only becomes a barrier through cornered resource, process power or switching costs; its evidence is that every durable data advantage on inspection turns out to be one of those three, and data-rich firms without them get copied. The conditional-data position replies that a self-reinforcing loop with slow decay and a high density threshold is structurally distinct from any of the seven and deserves its own name; its evidence is the persistence of advantage in domains where the loop is tight. What would have to be true for the orthodox view to be wrong: a documented case of a durable advantage resting on data where no contractual exclusivity, no operational pipeline and no switching cost can be identified. Such cases are surprisingly hard to produce, which is why the orthodox view still has the better of it in enterprise settings.

Will base-model progress eat proprietary-data advantages? The bitter-lesson position holds that it eats almost everything, and its evidence is three consecutive generations of vertical fine-tuning advantages evaporating, exactly as Figure 3's red line shows. The outcome-data position holds that the frontier can only absorb what is written down somewhere, and that private outcome labels — who defaulted, who churned, which intervention worked — are absent from every corpus by construction. What would have to be true for the outcome position to be wrong: either that synthetic or simulated outcomes reach a fidelity that substitutes for real ones in a regulated decision, or that the labs acquire private outcome data directly through partnerships at scale. The second is not fanciful, and it is the single most important thing for a company like Yashvi to monitor.

Does distribution decide vertical AI? Steelmanned, the distribution case is strong: the incumbent bundles at zero marginal price, buyers satisfice, and a 20 percent quality edge rarely survives a procurement process that values one fewer vendor. Steelmanned, the quality case is also strong in exactly the domains where being wrong is expensive and attributable — lending, clinical, safety — because there the buyer has a named individual who carries the consequence. The disagreement resolves empirically per market, and the test is whether a specific human being's name is attached to the decision the model influences. Where there is such a person, quality wins more often than the distribution school predicts.

Is licensing your model moat-destroying or moat-reinforcing? The reinforcing case, descending from the commoditise-your-complement logic, is that licensing sets a de facto standard, grows the pie, and returns telemetry that widens your own loop. The destroying case is that in two-sided markets you are funding a rival's liquidity with your own scarcest asset. What would have to be true for the reinforcing case to hold at Yuvraj: that the licensee's customers are not substitutes for your own marketplace supply, and that the licence returns usable data rather than merely cash. Neither condition held. In other structures — a pure tooling company, say — both often do, which is why competent practitioners disagree about this in general and should not disagree about it in a specific case where the two conditions can simply be checked.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic can name the seven powers, can recite the thin-wrapper critique, and will tell you that data is a moat "if it compounds." Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways. They convert every defensibility conversation into a schedule with a number of months attached, because they know a moat is a rate of erosion rather than a binary. They instrument the rival's curve, not only their own, and can tell you what fraction of your data a competitor needs to become good enough rather than equal. They treat contract clauses, consent artefacts and randomised holdouts as product decisions with roadmap slots and owners, because those are the parameters that money cannot later buy. And they are willing to say out loud that a defensible position is small — Yuvraj's 260 lanes, Yamini's 340 accounts — rather than inflating it, because the purpose of the analysis is to decide where to concentrate, and an analysis that concludes everything is defended has concluded nothing. The final tell is temporal: the expert asks the moat question at the seed stage, when the answer is cheap to act on, and treats the Series C version of the question as a reporting exercise rather than a discovery.

12What each decided

Devika Raghunathan did not claim in the Series C meeting that Yashvi's data was unassailable. She put Figure 2 on the screen and said the company's parity exposure was roughly twenty-six months, decomposed into three months of application accrual, eleven months of label seasoning and about nine months of contract renegotiation that the rival could not skip. She then committed to spending those twenty-six months on two things that are not data at all: making Yashvi's output the object of record in the credit-committee file, which converts an accuracy advantage into a consequence-based switching cost; and extending the model-improvement clause to the four holdout lenders as a condition of their next renewal, which is the only parameter still under her control. The Series C closed in November 2026 at ₹2,480 crore pre-money — below the ask, and priced on retention rather than on the data-volume story.

Nandita Iyer took the counter-proposal to the TMS vendor: ETA and check-call automation licensed for ₹27 crore over three years, lane pricing withheld. The vendor accepted in principle and asked for pricing again in year two. Iyer's internal memo conceded that she had accepted ₹19 crore less for a position she could not prove, and argued that the ₹19 crore was the premium on an option whose value depended on whether Yuvraj could push its live band from 260 lanes to 600 before the vendor built its own. Both decisions are defensible and neither is obviously right, which is the ordinary condition of this class of judgement.

Discussion questions

  1. Yashvi's advantage rests substantially on contract clauses signed in 2022 by founders with no leverage. Is that a cornered resource in Helmer's sense, or is it a one-time historical accident that a rival will eventually route around — and what evidence, observable in the next four quarters, would distinguish the two?
  2. Iyer withheld lane pricing to protect a band covering 23 percent of trips, forgoing ₹19 crore. Construct the strongest case that she was wrong: under what conditions on the licensee's customer base and on Yuvraj's own lane-expansion rate does taking the full ₹46 crore dominate?
  3. Yamini Studio's defensible asset — a brand-asset library and an approval workflow — was buildable in month three and was built in month twenty. What organisational mechanism, rather than what insight, would have caused that library to be built early, and what would it have cost the company in speed at the moment it mattered most?

13Going deeper

Moats and the 7 Powers
The parent framework this page applies. Reading it directly gives you the discipline of naming which power an advantage instantiates, which is the single question that stops "we have data" from passing unchallenged.
Adding an LLM feature
Understanding exactly how little engineering a competent LLM feature requires is what makes the parity arithmetic intuitive rather than theoretical; it unlocks a realistic estimate of r for any rival.
Feedback loops and data flywheels
The mechanics of instrumenting the loop this page assumes — label joins, retraining cadence, holdouts, drift monitoring — and the difference between a loop that compounds and a dashboard that only looks like one.
AI as a strategy, not a feature
Takes the argument up a level: what changes about the business model, pricing and org design when the four parameters become the company's operating plan rather than a defensibility slide.
Moats when features are cheap to copy
Generalises beyond AI to any environment with collapsed imitation costs, and connects directly to Teece's complementary-assets logic used in Section 2.
Competitive analysis
Gives you the evidence base for estimating a rival's flow ratio and data rights rather than guessing them — the practical bottleneck in every calculation above.
Right to win
Reframes the same question from the inside: not what stops them, but why us — and it is the check that prevents a defensible but tiny position from becoming the strategy.
Network effects
Essential for the marketplace case, where the AI layer amplifies liquidity rather than creating advantage; it explains why Yuvraj's parameters are all downstream of matching density.
Switching costs and lock-in
Develops the distinction between friction-based and consequence-based lock-in from Nuance Six, which is the conversion Raghunathan committed her next twenty-six months to.
Positioning
Determines which decision unit you are defending in the first place; a positioning choice is implicitly a choice about where your density threshold has to be cleared.
Five forces and industry structure
Supplies the layer above the firm: whether the surplus your moat protects is available to be captured at all, or is being competed away at the industry level regardless of who wins.

Moats in the AI Era: The Nirmal Renewal

Ninaad Voice Analytics · Madurai, Tamil Nadu · 25 September 2026
A teaching case on competitive strategy for AI-era products.

1. Opening

On the morning of 25 September 2026, Osheen Kalyanasundaram sat in the third-floor conference room of Ninaad Voice Analytics' Madurai office and reread an email from Ananya Krishnamurthy, Head of Collections at Nirmal General Insurance in Chennai. Nirmal's renewal committee would meet on 6 October, the Monday after Dussehra, to decide whether to renew its contract with Ninaad or move its 400-seat collections floor to a new vendor, Naadi Speech Cloud, which had quoted a price nearly 40 percent lower for what it called an equivalent product. Osheen, Ninaad's VP of Product, had ten working days to decide what Ninaad would offer Nirmal, and by extension, whether Ninaad had a business worth defending at its current prices at all.

2. Company background

Ninaad Voice Analytics was founded in Madurai in 2019 to solve a narrow problem: contact centres serving Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Maharashtra, and West Bengal had no reliable way to transcribe and audit agent calls in regional languages and their dialects. Global speech vendors handled English and, unevenly, Hindi; Tamil from rural Madurai, Marathi from Vidarbha, or Bengali from north Bengal produced transcripts too poor for quality monitoring or regulatory compliance. Ninaad built automatic transcription and call-quality scoring for five languages — Tamil, Telugu, Hindi, Marathi and Bengali — sold to BPO operators such as Teleperformance India and WNS, and to the in-house collections and support centres of banks and insurers such as Bajaj Allianz and HDFC Bank, who needed to prove to the RBI and IRDAI that mandatory disclosures were read out correctly on every call. By 2026 Ninaad had 140 clients, roughly ₹38 crore in annual recurring revenue, and nearly nine million human-corrected call transcripts collected over five years, used to continually retrain its models. Nirmal General Insurance, a mid-sized Chennai insurer with a 400-agent collections operation, was one of Ninaad's oldest accounts, worth ₹1.92 crore a year and closely watched by prospects as a reference.

3. The situation

In August, Naadi Speech Cloud, a Hyderabad startup founded fourteen months earlier by two former data scientists from a large IT services firm, began approaching Ninaad's clients directly. Naadi's product looked, on a demo screen, almost identical to Ninaad's: automatic transcription, sentiment tagging, a dashboard of flagged calls. Its engineering was thin by design — it called an open multilingual speech model trained under the government's Bhashini initiative and IIT Madras's AI4Bharat project, added a large language model for summarisation, and wrapped both in a clean interface, at a fraction of Ninaad's engineering cost. Naadi's pitch to Ananya was blunt: the underlying speech models were now public goods, so paying a premium for a proprietary vendor no longer made sense.

Osheen's team was split on how alarmed to be. Preethi Ilangovan, Ninaad's Head of ML Engineering in Bengaluru, argued that Naadi's demo would look fine on the clean, urban-accented calls startups use for pitches, but that Nirmal's actual volume was dominated by rural and small-town customers whose speech Naadi's off-the-shelf model had never been tuned on. Karan Bhatia, Ninaad's data scientist in Toronto, had spent two weeks building a blind benchmark of 3,000 real Nirmal calls, run through both systems, to test that claim directly. Rohan Mascarenhas, Sales Head in New Jersey, warned that whatever the numbers showed, three other prospects — including a large BPO evaluating Ninaad for a Dubai-based collections process — had already asked why Naadi was so much cheaper, and the pricing question would not stay contained to Nirmal.

4. The people

Osheen Kalyanasundaram — VP of Product, Ninaad Voice Analytics, Madurai
Must recommend, by 3 October, what Ninaad offers Nirmal and how it frames its position more broadly. Wants an answer grounded in evidence, not panic.
Preethi Ilangovan — Head of ML Engineering, Bengaluru
Believes the five years of human-corrected transcripts and the retraining loop built on them are the company's real asset, and resists treating the product as a commodity to be discounted.
Karan Bhatia — Data Scientist, Toronto
Wants the decision to rest on the benchmark he ran, not on intuition, and is wary of both over-claiming Ninaad's edge and dismissing Naadi too quickly.
Rohan Mascarenhas — Sales Head, New Jersey
Owns the revenue number and the wider pipeline; wants to protect the Nirmal account and is open to matching price if that closes the renewal.
Ananya Krishnamurthy — Head of Collections, Nirmal General Insurance, Chennai
Under pressure from her CFO to cut vendor costs, but personally accountable if a switch causes compliance flags to be missed on live calls.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — Nirmal General Insurance: current contract vs. Naadi's quote (400 seats)

Exhibit 2 — Karan's benchmark: transcription word-error rate and compliance-flag accuracy on 3,000 real Nirmal calls

Exhibit 3 — Where the moat actually sits. Naadi occupies the low-defensibility corner: its base model is available to any buyer directly. Ninaad's model layer alone is only slightly more defensible, but its labeled data, retraining loop, and client-specific compliance taxonomy — largely undersold in its current pitch — are what the benchmark in Exhibit 2 is really measuring.

6. The options

  1. Match Naadi's price for Nirmal, and pre-emptively lower list price for the segment. This protects the account and removes the pricing objection from the three other live deals Rohan is chasing. The cost is roughly ₹77 lakh a year in lost margin on Nirmal alone, a precedent that every renewal for the next two years will open with a discount demand, and no answer to what Ninaad is worth beyond the model call it makes.
  2. Hold price, and make the data and workflow moat visible and contractual. Share the benchmark in Exhibit 2 directly with Ananya, and offer a joint programme to extend the compliance taxonomy to a new product line Nirmal is launching, in exchange for a two-year term at a modest 12–15 percent discount rather than 40 percent. This trades some margin for longer lock-in and puts the real asymmetry — dialect accuracy and compliance precision — in front of the one person personally exposed if it goes wrong. The risk is that Nirmal's CFO overrules her on cost alone, and ten days may not be enough to build the case.
  3. Restructure Ninaad's own cost base around the same open models Naadi uses, and re-point engineering investment at the data and workflow layer. Swap the underlying transcription model for a cheaper open one where accuracy parity already exists (urban-call WER, Exhibit 2), cutting cost enough to match Naadi's price sustainably, while investing the savings in the correction loop and compliance taxonomy that are harder to copy. This is the most strategically honest response to a commoditising model layer, but it is a multi-quarter effort that cannot finish before 6 October, and it concedes, for now, that the model layer alone was never Ninaad's moat.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, is Naadi Speech Cloud selling, and why is it inexpensive to build and easy for others to copy?
  2. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, which parts of Ninaad's product are genuinely defensible, and which are a thin layer over a model anyone can access?
  3. If Osheen chooses Option 2, what would Ananya need to see or hear, beyond the benchmark numbers, to recommend staying with Ninaad to her CFO?
  4. Is Option 3 a admission that Ninaad's current pricing has been wrong all along, or a natural evolution of where a defensible business should sit once the model layer commoditises?

8. A note for the learner

This case turns on a distinction the "moats in the AI era" lens exists to make: a wrapper around a model is not a business, because the model is available to any competitor on the same terms — Exhibit 3 places Naadi exactly there, and its urban-call word-error rates in Exhibit 2 confirm a generic model, competently wrapped, now looks competitive in a demo. What Ninaad actually owns is different in kind: nine million human-corrected transcripts feeding a continuous retraining loop, and a compliance-flag taxonomy tuned over three years to Nirmal's own scripts. Exhibit 2's dialect-call numbers and the compliance-precision gap are direct evidence this data is not decorative — it produces a result a thin wrapper cannot match without years of the same corrected volume, which a fourteen-month-old startup does not have and cannot buy.

A well-reasoned answer does not treat this as a pricing negotiation alone; it asks which asset the price is protecting. Option 1 defends revenue this quarter while conceding Ninaad's edge is only a marketing claim, inviting the same demand from every other account. Option 3 correctly reads where the durable advantage lives but cannot be executed inside Osheen's ten-day window. The defensible path is Option 2: put Exhibit 2's evidence directly in front of Ananya, who bears the compliance risk personally, trade a real but partial concession for a longer contract that raises switching cost, and use the account itself to widen the data moat further while the model layer is addressed on the longer timeline Option 3 requires. The reasoning that should survive into the boardroom: match price where the model layer has genuinely commoditised, but never discount the data and workflow layer as if it had.

Moats in the AI Era

Strategy & Business — Competitive Strategy & Moats · Why a thin model wrapper has no moat, and when "our data" is real

On the morning of 11 August 2026, Ananya Rai, VP of Product at Tanishka Health Cloud, opened her sales dashboard and watched the pilot-to-paid conversion rate for the company's flagship product fall from 61 percent to 37 percent in a single quarter. Tanishka Health Cloud, a thirty-month-old Bengaluru startup with sixty hospital customers across Karnataka, Maharashtra and Telangana, sold an AI-assisted clinical documentation and triage assistant: a tool that listened to a doctor's spoken consultation, produced a structured note in the hospital's electronic health record format, and flagged triage-relevant symptoms for the nursing desk. It had raised a ₹38 crore Series A in early 2024 on the strength of that product, and by mid-2026 was six weeks from closing a Series B term sheet with a Mumbai growth fund. The fund's lead investor had asked one question in every partner meeting: what stops a well-capitalised incumbent from copying this in a quarter?

Ananya's answer, until August, had been confident: nobody else had trained a clinical scribe on real, doctor-corrected Indian hospital dictation, mixing Hindi, English and regional languages, at Tanishka's scale. Then Talwar Health Systems — a twelve-year-old, ₹400-crore-ARR hospital information systems vendor already embedded in 340 hospitals across the country — watched a product demo at a health-IT conference in Hyderabad, licensed the same class of foundation model API that Tanishka used, and shipped a near-identical clinical scribe feature seven weeks later. Talwar bundled it free into its existing HIS contracts. Hospital administrators, who already paid Talwar for patient records, medicine ordering and billing, saw no reason to keep paying Tanishka for something that now arrived at no incremental cost. That was the quarter Ananya's conversion rate fell fourteen points, and it is the decision this page follows her through: does Tanishka actually have a moat, or did it spend thirty months building a feature that anyone with an API key and seven weeks could copy?

1The idea, defined precisely

A moat — in the sense strategists use the word — is a structural, durable reason a competitor cannot replicate your advantage even after they can see exactly what you built and want to copy it. The word is Warren Buffett's, borrowed from castle architecture and used in his shareholder letters from the 1980s onward to describe businesses protected from competition by something more than a head start. The idea was formalised for operating businesses by Hamilton Helmer in his 2016 book 7 Powers, which named seven specific mechanisms — scale economies, network effects, switching costs, branding, cornered resource, process power and counter-positioning — as the only structural reasons a competitor's superior resources and rational intent still fail to close a gap. Helmer's framework did not anticipate large language models, but it did not need to: the powers are mechanism-agnostic, and the arrival of cheap, rentable AI capability is best understood as a shock that has made some of those seven powers nearly free to build and has made others suddenly, urgently scarce.

The problem this idea solves for a product leader like Ananya is separating two things that look identical from the outside: a genuine, compounding advantage, and a temporary lead produced only by being first to notice an opportunity. Before generative AI, that distinction was often blurred by the sheer engineering effort a product required — building a competent search engine or a fraud model took years, so a lead of eighteen months felt safe even without a formal moat. Foundation models collapsed the engineering cost of producing a plausible-looking AI feature to a prompt, an API call and a weekend of UI work, which means the years-long head start that used to substitute for a real moat no longer exists by default. The one sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: a moat in the AI era is not the model you call, because everyone can rent the same brain — it is the structural reason your specific loop of proprietary data, distribution or switching cost keeps compounding after a well-funded rival copies your interface in six weeks.

2How it actually works

Testing whether an AI feature has a moat is a sequence of questions, and the sequence matters because skipping a step is exactly how teams like Ananya's early product team fooled themselves. The first question is a layer question: at what point in the stack does your product's value actually sit? A foundation-model API call sits at the bottom of the stack and is available to anyone with a credit card; a system prompt and a chat interface sit one layer up and are available to anyone who can read your marketing site and reverse-engineer your flow; a fine-tuned or distilled model sits higher still and requires training data and engineering time to reproduce; a proprietary, continuously-refreshed data pipeline sits higher again and requires relationships, consent and years to reproduce; and workflow lock-in — the point where switching costs your customer real operational pain — sits at the top and is the hardest layer of all to dislodge once built.

The second question is what practitioners usually skip: the thin-wrapper test. If a well-capitalised competitor saw only a screenshot of your feature — not your code, not your data, just the visible behaviour — how many weeks would it take them to replicate what the user experiences? For Tanishka's original scribe interface, the honest answer in early 2024 would have been six to eight weeks, and Talwar's actual seven-week replication in 2026 confirmed it. A feature that fails this test at "a few weeks" is not disqualified from having a moat, but it tells you the moat, if one exists, cannot be sitting in the interface — it has to be sitting somewhere the screenshot does not show.

The third question is the flywheel test: does using the product generate proprietary information that makes the product measurably better for the next user, in a way a competitor without that usage history cannot access? This is where the phrase "our data is the moat" gets tested rather than asserted. A genuine data flywheel requires four things to be true simultaneously, and Ananya's team learned to check all four rather than stopping at the first: the data must be proprietary, meaning it is not already inside the foundation model's training set and not for sale on the open market; it must be structurally hard to replicate, meaning a rival cannot simply buy, license or scrape an equivalent dataset; it must compound, meaning more usage produces measurably better output that draws more usage; and it must be applied where it changes an outcome the customer actually pays for — accuracy, cost or safety — rather than a cosmetic personalisation nobody notices. The final step, and the one general managers most often leave implicit, is mapping whatever survives that test back onto Helmer's seven powers, because "we have proprietary data" is not itself a power — it is only a power if it instantiates one, most often a cornered resource (data or relationships nobody else can get on any terms), process power (an operational pipeline for capturing and using the data that took years to tune and cannot be bought), or switching costs (the customer's own workflow now depends on your system in a way that makes leaving expensive).

Figure 1. Tanishka's scribe interface (layers 1–2) was exactly as defensible as Talwar's seven-week copy suggested — not at all. Whatever moat Tanishka has, if it exists, has to live in layers 3–5.

3A worked example, followed line by line

Ananya's team did not settle the boardroom question with adjectives; they settled it with a spreadsheet, and the arithmetic is worth walking through because it overturns the naive version of "we have thirty months of data, they have none." Tanishka's sixty hospitals produced roughly 1,200 patient encounters each per month, for a combined 72,000 AI-drafted clinical notes each month. In month one of deployment, back in early 2024, doctors materially corrected 34 percent of those AI-drafted notes — the model missed local terminology, mis-transcribed code-switched Hindi-English-Kannada dictation, and misclassified triage urgency often enough that doctors rewrote more than a third of what it produced. Every one of those corrections was captured, and once a month Tanishka's engineers fine-tuned a lightweight adapter on the accumulated corrected pairs. By September 2026, thirty months and roughly 1.8 million corrected transcripts later, the correction rate had fallen to 6 percent.

Translate that correction rate into money a hospital administrator actually feels, because that is the number that closes or loses a renewal. Each material correction costs a doctor about four minutes of review and rewriting; loaded physician time in Tanishka's hospital segment runs approximately ₹1,800 per hour, or ₹30 per minute. At Tanishka's current 6 percent correction rate, a single hospital with 1,200 encounters a month generates 72 corrections, consuming 288 minutes, or 4.8 hours, of doctor time — a monthly cost of roughly ₹8,640. Talwar, having launched with the same class of foundation model but no correction-and-fine-tuning pipeline of its own, was running at roughly the same 32 percent correction rate Tanishka had shown in month one. On the same 1,200-encounter hospital, that is 384 corrections, 1,536 minutes, 25.6 hours, and a monthly cost of roughly ₹46,080. That gap — ₹37,440 of doctor time saved per hospital per month — is a real, sellable, defensible number, and it is the number Ananya decided to put in front of the investor instead of a vague claim about "our data."

The second pass is the one that matters more, because it is the one that tells you whether the gap is actually a moat or just a head start. Suppose Talwar, stung by losing renewal conversations on that ₹37,440 figure, builds its own correction-capture-and-fine-tune pipeline starting this month. How long until it closes the gap? If Talwar's accuracy improves at the same rate Tanishka's did — a fall from roughly 32 percent to 6 percent driven by accumulating 1.8 million corrected transcripts — the question becomes how fast Talwar can accumulate that volume, not how many months have passed. Talwar has 340 hospitals, each producing roughly 1,200 encounters a month, or 408,000 encounters monthly, of which 32 percent generate a correction: 130,560 corrected transcripts every month. To reach Tanishka's 1.8 million, Talwar needs roughly fourteen months — less than half of the thirty months it took Tanishka, because Talwar's five-and-a-half-times larger hospital base lets it out-run Tanishka on raw volume even starting from zero. That single recalculation is what changed the argument Ananya brought to her board: the moat cannot be the pile of corrected transcripts, because a bigger rival can accumulate an equivalent pile faster than Tanishka accumulated its first one. If there is a moat here at all, it has to be something that stops Talwar from building the capture-and-fine-tune pipeline in the first place, not the data that pipeline would eventually produce.
